references.text: In the previous verse ("when he came to himself"), the prodigal son decides to return to his father. Verse 18 is the direct continuation of this decision – he formulates his confession ([ref:Luk 15:17|Luke 15:17]).

The prodigal son carries out what he planned in verse 18 and says word for word to his father: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you." This shows that the confession was brought forward in action ([ref:Luk 15:21|Luke 15:21]).

Pharaoh says to Moses and Aaron: "I have sinned against your God the Lord and against you." The expression to sin "against heaven and before you" in Luke 15:18 has a parallel in this double confession of sin against God and against people ([ref:2 Mos 10:16|Exodus 10:16]).

The people of Israel confess: "We have sinned, for we have spoken against the Lord and against you." The same structure with sin directed both against God and against a human being is reflected in the words of the prodigal son ([ref:4 Mos 21:7|Numbers 21:7]).

Saul says to Samuel: "I have sinned, for I have transgressed the Lord's command and your words." The confession of sin against God and against an authority figure is found in the prodigal son's admission ([ref:1 Sam 15:18|1 Samuel 15:18]).

Saul confesses: "I have sinned, for I have transgressed the Lord's command and your words." A parallel to the prodigal son's recognition of sin against heaven and against his father ([ref:1 Sam 15:24|1 Samuel 15:24]).

David confesses in his penitential psalm: "Against you, you only, have I sinned; what is evil in your eyes, that I have done." The prodigal son's confession of sin "against heaven" reflects this deep recognition that all sin ultimately is against God ([ref:Sal 51:6|Psalm 51:6]).

The prophet Jeremiah conveys the people's confession: "We have sinned against the Lord our God." This recognition of sin against God is a recurring theme in the Old Testament, echoed by the words of the prodigal son ([ref:Jer 3:25|Jeremiah 3:25]).

Daniel confesses: "We have sinned and done wrong." This humble confession of sin before God has thematic similarity with the prodigal son's willingness to return and confess his sin ([ref:Dan 9:5|Daniel 9:5]).

Jesus says that there is joy among God's angels over one sinner who repents. The prodigal son's decision to get up and go to his father is exactly such a repentance that creates joy in heaven ([ref:Luk 15:10|Luke 15:10]).

The tax collector beats his breast and prays: "God, be merciful to me, a sinner!" Both the tax collector and the prodigal son acknowledge their sin without excuses and cast themselves on God's mercy ([ref:Luk 18:13|Luke 18:13]).

"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just, so that he forgives us our sins." The prodigal son's confession to his father illustrates the principle that sincere confession of sin is met with forgiveness ([ref:1 Joh 1:9|1 John 1:9]).
